paper.title: A SINGLE ARCHITECTURE FOR REPRESENTING INVARIANCE UNDER ANY SPACE GROUP
paper.research_summary: This paper introduces the Crystal Fourier Transformer (CFT), a single neural architecture that adapts its weights to enforce exact invariance to any input crystallographic space group. It achieves this by constructing symmetry-adapted Fourier bases through analytical derivation of constraints that group operations impose on Fourier coefficients, encoding these constraints into a group-conditional routing matrix (adjacency matrix of a dual graph). The architecture enables weight sharing across all 230 space groups, supports zero-shot generalization to unseen groups, and is validated on material property prediction tasks.

tasks.task_name_raw: developing a single machine learning architecture that is capable of adapting its weights automatically to enforce invariance to any input space group
tasks.objective: Develop a single, adaptive neural architecture capable of enforcing exact invariance to any of the 230 crystallographic space groups.
target_properties: zero-shot generalization to unseen space groups
constraints: must support all 230 space groups in 3D
must enable weight sharing across groups
must overcome data sparsity for rare groups
output_goal: material property predictions (e.g., total energy, band gap)

evidence.text: In this work we present a new approach to crystallographic symmetries by developing a single machine learning architecture that is capable of adapting its weights automatically to enforce invariance to any input space group.
We introduce the Crystal Fourier Transformer (CFT), a model designed to process crystallographic data by explicitly building in invariance to its space group symmetry.

stages.stage_name_raw: acquiring crystal structure data with space group labels
stages.stage_goal: Obtain crystal structures annotated with their corresponding space group identifiers.
stage_output: dataset of crystals with atomic positions, lattice vectors, and space group IDs

evidence.text: For our primary benchmark experiments, we use data from the Materials Project, one of the largest databases of computational material properties (Jain et al., 2013).
For each material, the model receives the atomic numbers and fractional coordinates of atoms within the unit cell, the 3×3 lattice vectors, and the corresponding space group identifier (1-230).

stages.stage_name_raw: computing orbit distances for self-supervised pretraining
stages.stage_goal: Calculate ground-truth orbit distances dG(x1, x2) between atomic positions as supervision signal.

evidence.text:
The orbit distance is defined as
dG(x1, x2) := minϕ1,ϕ2∈G ||ϕ1(x1) −ϕ2(x2)||2.
(8)
It measures the shortest Euclidean distance between any two points in the respective orbits of the atoms, which stays invariant to applications of group actions to either atom.

stages.stage_name_raw: pretraining the G-invariant positional encoding module
stages.stage_goal: Train the symmetry-adapted encoding module to produce embeddings whose Euclidean distance matches the orbit distance.

evidence.text: We first validate this capability in a controlled, self-supervised setting before applying the model to downstream tasks. The goal is to train the encoder to produce positional encodings where the Euclidean distance between embeddings directly corresponds to the true orbit distance dG(x1, x2) between atoms.
The model is trained to minimize the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the L2 distance of the output embeddings and the ground-truth orbit distance.

stages.stage_name_raw: training the full Crystal Fourier Transformer (CFT)
stages.stage_goal: Train the complete CFT architecture on material property prediction tasks using pretrained positional encodings.

evidence.text: Having validated our encoding module, we now evaluate the full CFT architecture on the task of predicting material properties from the Materials Project dataset.
We use the pre-trained positional encoding model from Section 5.2 to initialize the positional encodings in CFT.

stages.stage_name_raw: evaluating CFT on material property prediction benchmarks
stages.stage_goal: Assess CFT's performance against state-of-the-art baselines on predicting total energy, band gap, bulk modulus, and shear modulus.
stage_output: test MAE scores for each property

evidence.text: The task is to predict four key material properties from the crystal structure: total energy (eV/atom), band gap (eV), bulk modulus (log GPa), and shear modulus (log GPa).

stages.stage_goal: Validate that CFT generalizes to held-out space groups without retraining by providing the precomputed routing matrix MG at inference time.

evidence.text: For CFT in the zero-shot regime, we simply provide at inference time the precomputed routing matrix MG corresponding to the unseen group G; no parameter updates or fine-tuning are performed.
